blocks.text: The Arabs teach the same. Damir, in the chapter On locusts, under the heading الحكم [al-ḥukm], that is, On use: اجمع المسلمون علي اباحة اكل الجراد [ajmaʿa al-muslimūn ʿalā ibāḥat akl al-jarād], "The Muslims agree that the eating of locusts is lawful." They rely, of course, on the authority of Abdalla, whose words are: غزونا مع رسول الله صلي الله عليه وسلم سبع غزوات ناكل الجراد فيها [ghazawnā maʿa rasūl Allāh ṣallā Allāh ʿalayhi wa-sallam sabʿ ghazawāt naʾkul al-jarād fīhā], "We undertook seven military expeditions with the prophet of God, on whom God be gracious, eating the flesh of locusts." Hence they keep saying that God sends them, sometimes to be رزقا القوم [rizqan li-l-qawm] food for the peoples, sometimes to be بلا علي القوم [balāʾ ʿalā al-qawm] a plague upon the peoples. Let these few examples, taken from Alcamus, suffice: الصراح طاير كالجندب يوكل [al-ṣurāḥ ṭāʾir ka-l-jundub yuʾkal], Sorrach, a small winged animal like the bruchus, which is eaten. جرد شري جلده عن اكله [jurida shariya jilduhu ʿan aklihi], Giarida, pustules broke out on his flesh because of eating it; that is, because of eating the locust mentioned before. جرد شكا بطنه من [col. 492] اكله [jurida shakā baṭnuhu min aklihi], Giurida, his belly ached from eating the same. المرتجل من يقع برجل من جراد فيشتوي منها [al-murtajil man yaqaʿ bi-rijl min jarād fa-yashtawī minhā], Almurtegilo, one who, coming upon a swarm of locusts, roasts them. الحنتف الجراد المنتف المنقي للطبخ [al-ḥantaf al-jarād al-muntaf al-munaqqā li-l-ṭabkh], Alchantapho, a locust that has been plucked and cleaned for cooking; الوهيسة ان يطبخ الجراد وتجفف ويدق ويخلط بدسم [al-wahīsa an yuṭbakh al-jarād wa-tujaffaf wa-yudaqq wa-yukhlaṭ bi-dasam], Alvvahisatho, when a locust is cooked, and after drying is pounded and mixed with fat: that is, to serve as food. Add to these the testimonies of more recent writers. Thus Nicolaus Clenardus in his Letters: "They bring wagons full of locusts into Fez; for here people commonly eat these enemies." And Leo Africanus [III, 332] book 9: "The desert of Arabia and the peoples of Libya regard their arrival as a happy omen: for they pound them into meal, either boiled or dried in the sun, and eat them." And Hermolaus Barbarus, Corollary 256 on Dioscorides: "Today too the Egyptians eat locusts" ^{(3)}.

But many write that the same is done in Judaea as well. Thus Bede, On the Holy Places ch. 14, reports that he learned from a holy bishop, Arculf, who had made a pilgrimage to those places, that "in Palestine there are very well-known locusts, which, with little bodies slight and short like a finger of the hand, are easily caught in the grass and, cooked in oil, provide a poor man's fare." And Euthymius on Matthew: "They say that to this very day in those parts many eat it (that kind of insect) dried in smoke, but that it has a strong smell and a bad taste." Jacques de Vitry too, bishop of Ptolemais, in the place cited above ^{b)}, testifies that in Judaea locusts were customarily eaten both fresh and preserved.

The sum of what we have said is this: besides the Acridophagi, known to all, the Nasamones too, and the people of Leptis, and the Parthians, and the Greeks, and the Hebrews once had locusts for food; as have the Arabs also, and the Numidians, and the Mauretanians, and the new inhabitants of Palestine, now for many centuries. Therefore that John ate locusts was nothing new or unheard of. What was singular in him was that in the desert he fed only on locusts and wild honey, and these perhaps as they chanced to come his way, not procured from elsewhere; so that the Jews might know that this man had an extraordinary office, and might be more attentive to his preaching. There was no reason, then, for Isidore of Pelusium to accuse of [III, 333] ignorance those who understand locusts here. Among their number were many far more celebrated than he: such as Theophilus of Antioch, Origen, Hilary and Chrysostom on Matthew; Ambrose on Luke; Clement of Alexandria, book 2 of the Paedagogus; Jerome, book 2 Against Jovinian and Letter 23 to Marcella; Augustine, book 10 of the Confessions, ch. 31. In short, all the writers older than Isidore, except only Paulinus in his sacred poem on John the Baptist; and against him it would be easy to set other Poets who agree with us. For thus Juvencus writes of him in book 1 of the Gospel History:
He who was wont [to eat] locusts in the country fields.
Accustomed to give his body a meagre fare of locusts and the liquid of wild honeycombs.
The Baptist, fed on locusts, bathes [them] in the river.
And Paul the Deacon in the Hymn On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist:
The camel provided a shaggy covering, [col. 493] sheep a girdle for his sacred limbs; for him water was drink, and food was honey joined with locusts.
